CD6 and its advisory body, Brooklyn Community Board 6 (CB6, also known as "the Board"), trace their roots to New York City's broader experiment with neighborhood governance. The 1963 City Charter formalized a structure for local planning, budgeting, and service delivery, establishing Community Planning Boards in all boroughs, with a total of 59. Meanwhile, the 1960s Little City Halls initiative, introduced by Mayor John Lindsay, established the role of District Managers to oversee local services. This framework was solidified by the 1975 City Charter and further strengthened by the 1989 Charter revisions, which affirmed Community Boards as vital institutions for addressing land use, budgetary, and service-related matters (NYC.gov, n.d.). Community Boards comprise an advisory body of 50 volunteer board members, aided by paid staff. Since 1975, this charter-created district has put its neighborhoods into direct relationship with one another. In its early years, it entrenched homeowner protectionism; in recent years, it has shifted towards a more progressive membership that advocates for housing, transportation, and climate equity.

Historically, this district and its board have been a leader in preservation and controlled growth: Cobble Hill, Park Slope, and Carroll Gardens were among the first historic districts created in New York City (1969-1973). Park Slope's 2003 rezoning was one of the first major contextual rezonings under Mayor Bloomberg, capping building dimensions to brownstone scales, approximately four or five stories. In the 2010s, the Park Slope Historic District expanded twice, making Park Slope the largest historic district by building count in New York City. These moves preserved the 19th-century rowhouse scale and "neighborhood character," but also tightly shrink-wrapped the development envelope, limiting opportunities for new housing on those blocks and increasing market viability by deterring change, reducing risk, and increasing home values. Historic district designations prevent demolitions and out-of-scale additions, regardless of available development rights, as determined by the Floor Area Ratio (FAR), which is the ratio of allowable building space to land area. This is a boon for architectural conservation, but also serves as another check on densification.

At the same time, CD6 contains Gowanus, with its infamous Gowanus Canal, designated a SUPERFUND site in 2010, and Red Hook. These industrial, low-density, low-elevation neighborhoods contain CD6's entire public housing (New York City Housing Authority | NYCHA), and are increasingly the sites of concentrated housing growth and rapid neighborhood change. The Gowanus Neighborhood Plan Rezoning (enacted in 2021) has begun to introduce new housing capacity along with a litany of community benefits, a win for citywide and local housing supply and neighborhood strategy advocates, with CB6’s advocacy for 100 percent affordable housing on the site’s publicly owned parcel (Gowanus Green) a particular bright spot.

This mix of highly constrained brownstone areas adjacent to upzoned growth areas makes CD6 an illuminating microcosm for studying the tensions between preservation and the need for housing amid a growing city-wide housing crisis. With a vacancy rate of less than two percent, the housing supply is at a decades-low level, decreasing affordability and tenant power, and leading to displacement.

Vast sections of CD6's residential neighborhoods remain governed by preservation-oriented rules that, in effect, have underperformed in these medium-density neighborhoods, causing them to functionally evolve into lower-density districts through regulations that have both limited physical growth and market and policy incentives that have altered the interior capacity of rowhouses.

This project represents a collaboration with CB6 to analyze the scope and policy implications of unit consolidations across the district, as observed and problematized by members of the Board's Land Use, Landmarks, and Housing Committee in recent years. It seeks to explore how 21st-century zoning and preservation decisions, layered on top of 20th-century zoning introductions and historic district designations, have influenced housing availability and equity, particularly through the lens of unit loss in historic districts and the constraints imposed by contextual rezonings in relation to the housing gains made through upzonings.

This study asks: How have past policies influenced affordability in CD6, and enabled or undermined equitable neighborhood change? Do the changes in units across neighborhoods interact with one another, creating a tradeoff that can lead to intended outcomes of increased access and affordability? How have overlapping land use restrictions altered the spatial distribution of housing growth and risk exposure in Brooklyn CD6? Finally, how can CB6 use its advisory powers to better influence outcomes moving forward? And how might the lessons from CD6 be employed to redefine development patterns amid citywide housing shortages?

The consequences of policy choices are visible, but contested: CD6's affluent, resource-rich neighborhoods have largely insulated themselves from new development, raising equity concerns among some community members – are these neighborhoods "sharing the burden" of new housing growth?--while others point to the success of recent rezonings to show that the district has contributed to citywide housing needs, and that preservation in some areas can continue and expand if housing elsewhere can compensate (Park Slope Civic Council, 2023).

This paper argues that CD-wide assessments and a narrative that every upzoning needs to be accompanied by a downzoning obscure the loss of units as multiple apartments in a rowhouse are consolidated into fewer units, further missing the opportunity to gently increase the housing inventory in neighborhoods. Indeed, the upzone-here/downzone-there redistributes risk—social, economic, and environmental—across the district, creating distinct “riskscapes” (Davies et al.) that shape who bears the burdens and benefits of neighborhood change according to sociopolitical power and privilege.

CD6 offers a compelling unit of analysis due to its unique blend of historic brownstone districts and industrial zones, uplands and lowlands, transit-oriented neighborhoods and transit deserts, as well as wealthy enclaves and large public housing populations. The district is mixed-use, mixed-eras, mixed-density, and topographically varied, ranging from (originally) marshland to hilltops, and now one of the most desirable (thus affluent) areas to live in the city. Neighborhoods within the district have distinct development histories that inform their current use and vulnerabilities, particularly as climate change impacts become an increasing risk. Superstorm Sandy in 2012 laid bare the importance of elevation in storm response, with low-lying neighborhoods like Red Hook and Gowanus devastated by the storm, while nearby brownstone neighborhoods like Park Slope and Carroll Gardens were lightly impacted. Successive storms, from Ophelia to Henri, have reinforced how risk (climate-related and displacement-related) is spatially offloaded.

CB6 is also a politically connected and powerful board, with the district's elected leaders ascending to the City's highest offices (including Mayor De Blasio and Comptroller Brad Lander), and the district boasting the highest local voter turnouts in New York City (FAC, 2021). Wealth, access, and opportunity in the district are spatially distributed by neighborhood, with risk generally downhill, and the most at-risk populations pushed offline. What happens here will have a citywide audience.

The period from 2003 to 2024, spanning from Mayor Bloomberg's post-9/11 reinvention of New York City through the current Adams administration, captures the implementation of the Park Slope contextual rezoning and culminates with the City Council's passage of the City of Yes for Housing Opportunity (COYHO | “City of Yes”). During these 20 years, the district has experienced pronounced housing gains along upzoned corridors and neighborhoods, but at the same time, consolidation, particularly in its brownstone neighborhoods. Anecdotal experiences conveyed to the Board–including over 120-unit losses recorded from CB6 Landmarks applications since 2013, or an average of one loss per applicant–were validated and amplified by data. According to the City of New York (NYC) Department of City Planning (DCP), CD6 lost 1,500 units from 2010-2024 alone, not including demolitions, the highest consolidation in Brooklyn and fourth-most in the city—following Manhattan CDs 2, 7, and 8 (respectively, SoHo/NoHo, Upper West Side, Upper East Side). For scale, that loss is equivalent to the unit count of roughly three Brooklyn Towers, the eye-catching Downtown Brooklyn skyscraper that can be seen from Lower Manhattan. COVID also produced increased consolidations in CD6: the district lost the most units to consolidation from 2020 to 2024 (approximately 400) than any other district in New York City. The City's policy regime, whether knowingly or not, facilitated these market outcomes, partially through the relative ease and cost differentials of consolidating townhouses versus new development, as well as the existing stock versus newly built stock. As Madden and Marcuse articulate in In Defense of Housing: The Politics of Crisis (2016), conditions in the housing market, as dictated by real estate capitalization rather than housing need, create chronic instability, with exceptions to the rule occurring under "economically irrational" actors. Expecting scalable irrationality in the face of government-backed market incentives is not sound housing policy; instead, it connotes market failure.

Consolidation, unlike new development, is fast, individualized, and largely unregulated. But its impact can be substantial, shifting housing stock availability for buyers and renters alike, privileging the hyper-luxury market. Unlike large-scale development, which is subject to public review, environmental analysis, and land use approvals, the combining of apartments or the conversion of multifamily buildings to single-family homes can proceed through simple alteration permits. This creates a skewed policy in which housing loss is expedited while housing addition is heavily regulated.

Focusing the City's growth policies on new development in rezoned industrial districts represents a numbers game of net units that fails to consider the location, size, typology, and economic considerations of unit changes. It also fails to consider how the influx of supply near, but not within, desired neighborhoods effectively impacts quality of life. Net unit figures don't account for the fact that losses occur in elevated, climate-resilient, transit- and amenity-rich areas. Furthermore, the recent policy tools of Mandatory Inclusionary Housing (MIH, 2016) and Universal Affordability Preference (UAP, 2024) are rarely applicable in these constrained areas due to bulk, height, and setback restrictions that limit as-of-right developments to a scale that qualifies for these programs. Neighborhood character, once defined by both social and architectural diversity, has been reduced to facade preservation and height conformity.

Rowhouses (brownstones and townhouses) dominate much of the district's landscape. (See Figure 2.) Many have the capacity to contain accessory apartments and historically have done so. This form of housing could naturally support "missing middle" units – such as duplexes, triplexes, garden apartments, or accessory dwelling units – without altering the human-scale character of the neighborhood. However, over the study period, the opposite trend has largely prevailed: numerous rowhouses have been converted into luxurious single-family residences, effectively reducing the district's housing supply. The research emphasizes that this outcome is not merely a product of market demand for luxury homes, but also a reflection of policy constraints.

This imbalance in regulatory treatment has quietly incentivized unit reductions – a phenomenon sometimes referred to as the "mansionization" of brownstones – at the expense of housing opportunities for multiple households. By highlighting this dynamic, the study frames the rowhouse not as an immutable, maximally utilized structure, but as a flexible housing resource that policy has constrained in one direction.

An argument made here is that modest modifications and adaptive re-use of existing buildings (e.g., splitting a large home into two apartments, finishing a basement as an accessory unit, or adding a carriage house in the rear yard) could provide significant new housing options without disrupting neighborhood character. These forms of incremental growth would be barely perceptible in the streetscape through the built environment, but could be visible by increasing diversity, the urban mix, or in Jane Jacobs' terminology, the "sidewalk ballet" of spontaneous interactivity.

Through this lens, the study posits that the "missing middle" housing, typically a desired addition to low-density neighborhoods for gentle densification, was present in CD6 throughout the 20th century, but is disappearing piecemeal. (See Figure 3.) Despite the medium-density zoning in CD6’s historic neighborhoods and the existing built environment's capacity to absorb additional density, policy choices are putting the missing middle housing typologies, which were lost to consolidations, in danger, removing a vital asset that the City has spent years and resources creating. Reclaiming it will require a comprehensive assessment of the housing environment and targeted changes to those policies.

Finally, the study connects the local lessons from CD6 to citywide housing initiatives, particularly Mayor Adams' City of Yes for Housing Opportunity plan (adopted by the City Council in late 2024), which is a sweeping set of zoning amendments aimed at easing New York's housing shortage by "making it possible to build a little more housing in every neighborhood." The plan encompasses many of the strategies that this thesis identifies as lacking in CD6's recent history. For example, a key component of City of Yes is legalizing accessory dwelling units (ADUs) – such as basement apartments and backyard cottages – which are currently prohibited in one- and two-family homes under the city’s Zoning Resolution. This policy change directly addresses the potential for gentle infill in rowhouse neighborhoods, empowering homeowners to create small additional units that provide income for owners and new housing for renters, all while maintaining the neighborhood’s scale. However, historic and contextual zoning districts have been largely excluded from these reforms.

This report argues that if CD6 is to advance policies leading to equitable neighborhood change, focusing on fostering income, racial and ethnic diversity, avoiding displacement, increasing opportunity, and densifying in less climate vulnerable, amenity-rich areas, policies must move beyond aesthetic preservation to prioritize housing function, economic realities, social resilience, and inclusive urban form, and puts forth a challenge to implement additional housing supply and affordability measures to the toolkit in addition to upzoning. The district's experience demonstrates that preservation and housing creation need not be mutually exclusive, but achieving both requires more nuanced and intentional policy design.

My understanding of CD6’s housing dynamics is shaped by both professional and civic experience. I currently serve as the Land Use Coordinator for CB6. Previously, I served as a board member for four years, during which I voted in favor of the Gowanus Neighborhood Plan, which is bringing new housing to the district (including 3,000 units of affordable housing), capital funding to NYCHA’s Gowanus and Wyckoff Houses campuses, stormwater capture infrastructure, dramatically improved sewer infrastructure, and activating a neighborhood that is at the center of CD6. Since September 2024, I have held one of two CB6 seats on the Brooklyn Marine Terminal Task Force.

I also worked in real estate throughout Brooklyn’s brownstone neighborhoods during the height of the COVID-19 market run-up—a period defined by competitive bidding, all-cash offers, and rapid price acceleration for brownstones, alongside simultaneous volatility in the rental market. These roles exposed me to the policy blind spots that enabled townhouse consolidation, the market incentives driving speculative purchases, and the disconnect between regulatory intent and on-the-ground housing outcomes. This experience informs both the questions I am posing and my insights into the systems I’m analyzing: the NYC Zoning Resolution, NYC Department of Buildings approvals, NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission oversight, and the rational behavior of market actors responding to an uneven and opaque regulatory landscape.

To achieve its objectives, this paper employs a research design that combines spatial data analysis, sociodemographic analysis, policy review, and historical research, all framed by a literature review of housing theory in New York City, encompassing reports by influential think tanks and recent academic theses. The study primarily focuses on the years 2003 to 2024, from the passage of the Park Slope Contextual Rezoning under Mayor Bloomberg through the passage of City of Yes under Mayor Adams. A quantitative analysis of housing unit changes forms the foundation, utilizing the treasure trove of New York City’s open-source data, as well as data from the Decennial Census and the American Community Survey. NYC Department of Buildings permits for housing changes (AltLoss, identified as unit consolidation hereafter, and AltGain, indicating an increase in Certificate of Occupancy) for new buildings, demolitions, and other types of construction gathered and updated by the NYC Department of City Planning were analyzed in ArcGIS Pro to identify spatial patterns. This was overlaid with PLUTO land use data, NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission historic districts, New York Zoning Map Amendment zoning overlays, Federal Emergency Management Agency flood maps, subway walksheds, and mapping of tree canopy density (NYC Department of Parks and Recreation), school districts (NYC Department of Education), supermarkets, and banks (ArcGIS Business Analyst). This dataset was available from 2010 to 2024. For housing change from 2003 to 2010, U.S. Census data on net housing change, which is not disaggregated by change like the Department of Buildings dataset, infer areas of loss versus gain from that period. Spatialized housing data was also overlaid with American Community Survey data on racial, ethnic, and income distribution, including inequality indices like the Racial Diversity Index and Income Diversity Ratio, as well as tracking changes in median household income, median sale and rent prices, and comparisons to contemporary Area Median Incomes for regional comparison. This spatial approach revealed patterns such as clusters of rowhouse unit mergers or the limited pockets of new housing construction.

In parallel, a detailed policy and zoning history of CD6 was carried out, reviewing rezoning maps, CB6 records, and Landmarks Preservation Commission (LPC)-designated Historic District expansions to understand the regulatory context for each time period. Analysis of zoning regulations (such as density restrictions and special permit requirements) and building codes discerns why specific changes (like adding an extra unit in a brownstone) are constrained. By comparing the processes for unit addition versus unit removal, the research illuminates how rules have made it far easier to combine apartments than to create new ones.

This approach balances granular, on-the-ground changes (such as housing units gained or lost on specific lots) with broader policy frameworks. By triangulating between maps, data, and policy documents, the study creates a comprehensive view of how policy decisions at both local and citywide levels have influenced neighborhood change. Central to this inquiry is the idea that CD6’s iconic rowhouse typology represents a missed opportunity for gentle density and adaptive reuse under current policies.

The situation in CD6 vividly illustrates the need for these changes. If an owner in Carroll Gardens today wanted to convert a spacious three-story brownstone into, say, three separate apartments or add a basement ADU, they would likely hit multiple bureaucratic and legal obstacles – yet nothing stopped a neighboring brownstone owner from converting three units into one lavish home. The City of Yes aims to address some imbalances by removing development obstacles and offering incentives to encourage housing development through zoning. However, carve-outs for historic districts and contextual rezonings, as discussed in the Analysis section, may dampen their efficacy in CD6’s highest loss neighborhoods.

By examining CD6’s outcomes under the old policy regime, this thesis provides grounded evidence to inform such reforms. It shows how a lack of “missing middle” options has contributed to affordability pressures and exclusion in one community, and by extension, how enabling modest growth citywide could help. In quantitative terms, if a policy like City of Yes had been in place, CD6 might have added units instead of losing 1,500 in the early 2010s. More broadly, the research findings support the idea that meeting New York City’s ambitious housing targets will require both large-scale developments and small-scale, context-sensitive infill.

Brooklyn CD6 exemplifies many affluent, transit-accessible neighborhoods where significant new developments are rare; unlocking housing potential in such areas is crucial for a fair and effective response to the housing crisis. By focusing on CD6, this research not only clarifies the local consequences of zoning and preservation policies but also underscores their relevance to citywide housing policy. The purpose of the study, ultimately, is to inform how the government of New York City (“the City”) can address its housing crisis through a more balanced approach – one that recognizes the value of its existing neighborhood fabric and seeks to carefully integrate new “missing middle” housing opportunities within that fabric, rather than allowing that potential to remain missing.

The project maps unit loss across CD6 using Department of Buildings (DOB) permit data and tax lot files, overlaid with zoning and floodplain boundaries. LPC-designated historic districts and contextual zoning overlays are analyzed in conjunction with elevation and risk maps to identify spatial discrepancies. LPC filings are used to identify patterns of housing reduction that pass through regulatory review but do not appear in broader planning discussions. Where possible, citywide findings (e.g., from Brodheim, 2023) are localized to the CD6 context. Overlays convey context, but not statistical significance.

DOB alteration permit data is only available from 2010 onward; as a result, this project is unable to directly document consolidation activity between 2003 and 2010. For this earlier period, demographic and housing stock changes are inferred from U.S. Census data. While this offers valuable insight into broader shifts, it does not provide parcel-level detail or direct evidence of unit loss. DOB alteration permits do not always accurately specify the number of units removed or added, and some unit consolidations may occur without permits or through filings that cannot be reliably geocoded.

This paper aims to establish context, present and analyze findings, and then propose recommendations. The background chapter provides historic information on CD6’s neighborhoods, as well as zoning changes and the role of CB6 within those changes.
The literature review situates CD6’s historical context and contested future within the spirited and active debates on housing in New York City’s political discourse.

BACKGROUND Brooklyn Community District 6 (CD6) spans New York City’s most historically layered and politically engaged neighborhoods. It includes Park Slope, Carroll Gardens, Cobble Hill, Red Hook, Gowanus, and the Columbia Street Waterfront District. (See Figure 1 in the prior chapter.) Each area has a distinguishing architectural identity and demographic trajectory, shaped by waves of immigration, industrial growth and decline, infrastructure development, policy interventions from Urban Renewal to historic preservation, and a topography that ranges from hilltops to landfill of marshes.
Early History: Lenape Land to Dutch Farmland

Before European colonization, the area that now comprises CD6 was home to the Lenape people, who lived with the region's wetlands, forests, and streams. The waterways that define the district, such as Gowanus Creek, provided a vital source of food and transportation. In the 17th century, Dutch settlers began to purchase and colonize the area, converting its fertile marshlands into farmland. Dutch families, such as the Van Brunts and Litchfields, established agricultural estates. Gristmills powered by the region’s creeks became vital to the local economy (Alexiou, 2015).
19th Century Growth: Industrialization and Brownstone Neighborhoods

Brooklyn experienced rapid urbanization in the 19th century, driven by the Industrial Revolution and Gowanus’ proximity to Manhattan. Gowanus Creek was converted into the Gowanus Canal (1853-1874) to serve as a significant industrial channel (Alexiou, 2015). Gowanus then spurred the growth of its adjoining neighborhoods by providing the staging area for the raw material and the labor needed to construct “Brownstone” (northwest) Brooklyn, followed by diversifying as the “power district” for Brownstone Brooklyn, including oil and coal delivery and storage and a power plant. Park Slope, as well as the adjoining neighborhoods west of the Canal, collectively known then as “South Brooklyn,” have become desirable residential areas with tree-lined streets and architecturally significant homes (Alexiou, 2015).
20th Century Challenges: Industrial Decline and Urban Change

By the mid-1900s, the same industries that had fueled the area’s prosperity were in sharp decline. Red Hook’s deep-water docks lost cargo to containerized shipping at newer, rail-connected ports such as Newark, New Jersey. In Red Hook, the Atlantic Basin’s cargo operations closed, leaving thousands jobless. Gowanus’s factories shuttered or downsized, while decades of unregulated discharge made the Gowanus Canal one of the nation’s most polluted waterways (Alexiou, 2015). During this period, the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) erected its two largest local campuses—the Red Hook Houses (1938) and the Gowanus Houses (1949)—as relocation sites for families displaced by Urban Renewal demolition (Bloom, 2016). Tight tenant selection rules, “white flight,” and chronic underfunding soon concentrated low-income households in aging buildings that, by the 1970s, were already showing signs of physical and social distress (Dagen-Bloom, 2015). Meanwhile, Fourth Avenue, once dubbed the “Park Avenue of Brooklyn,” lost its landscaped median and drew auto-oriented uses after the subway cut was completed in 1915, earning notoriety by mid-century as a “Canyon of Mediocrity” (Nonko, 2015). Beginning in the 1960s, professionals and artists “rediscovered” the district’s rowhouses, sparking a “brownstone revival” in Cobble Hill (landmarked 1969), Carroll Gardens (1971), and Park Slope (1973). Fresh off the creation of LPC and the first historic district designation in 1968 (of nearby Brooklyn Heights), these new designations offered moderate financial incentives for restoration and protection from large-scale redevelopment, but also facilitated tenant buyouts and eviction tactics publicized in guidebooks like You Don’t Have to Be Rich to Own a Brownstone (Brodheim, 2023). This wave of reinvestment laid the groundwork for the gentrification pressures that intensified in the decades to follow (Spellen, 2015).

Rising from the wooded crest of Prospect Park and sloping westward to the New York Harbor, Brooklyn’s Community District 6 compresses an extraordinary range of history and terrain into a compact footprint. At the top of the ridge, Park Slope, Carroll Gardens, and Cobble Hill display some of the city’s most intact 19th-century streetscapes—continuous rows of brownstones and carriage houses framed by mature trees, pocket parks, and church spires.The American Planning Association (APA) has rated Park Slope as one of its “Great Neighborhoods,” rating it in top ten lists consistently since 2007. Downslope, the land flattens into the tidal plains of Gowanus and Red Hook, where brick warehouses, iron bulkheads, and NYCHA superblocks speak to a century of maritime and industrial uses. This elevation change organizes everyday life: the ridge enjoys sweeping park frontage, multiple subway lines, and complete neighborhoods with a dense constellation of cafés, highly-rated schools, and cultural venues. The lowlands are the targeted spaces of rapid neighborhood change in the 21st century, where disused industrial space makes way for new residential and mixed uses. The result is a district where architectural heritage and civic amenities are layered directly onto the landscape, with topography itself narrating a story of affluence, industry, and resilience and the evolving edge between them.

This historically mixed-use, working-class area has long been defined by its namesake canal, once flanked by tanneries, factories, and warehouses. Over 100 combined stormwater/sewer and other outfalls contribute to biological pollution, which is exacerbated by the decades during which the pumping system to circulate canal water was not operational.

Despite the repair of the pump, federal Superfund designation, and a major cleanup of the most egregiously polluted sites, the canal bed, and the bulkheads, the canal remains one of the most polluted bodies of water in the nation. The Gowanus also suffered from industrial decline and environmental degradation, becoming notorious for its mob operations. The Gowanus Canal became infamous for its pollution, as decades of unregulated industrial discharge rendered it one of the most contaminated waterways in the country. (Alexiou, 2015)

Source: Curbed (2015). Fourth Avenue, one of Brooklyn’s major thoroughfares, represents the boundary between Park Slope and Gowanus. Once envisioned as the "Park Avenue of Brooklyn" due to its landscaped median and stately development in the early 20th century, it declined following the construction of the subway in 1915 and the removal of its central median. By the mid-20th century, it had become dominated by auto-oriented and industrial uses, earning the nickname “Canyon of Mediocrity” (Nonko, 2015). In 2003, the City upzoned sections of Fourth Avenue (primarily R6 to R8A) to direct growth from the contextually rezoned Park Slope to a transit-rich corridor. However, this initial rezoning lacked design controls, resulting in mid-rise towers with little architectural distinction or public realm improvement, and no affordable units.

In response to community criticism and the corridor’s underwhelming built results, a second rezoning was adopted in 2011 to require ground-floor commercial use and include active street wall requirements for new developments along Fourth Avenue. These adjustments aimed to improve the pedestrian experience and create a more continuous retail frontage, particularly around subway stations and key intersections. In 2021, portions of Fourth Avenue were again rezoned in the Gowanus Neighborhood Plan. This rezoning extended MIH requirements to previously upzoned parcels on Fourth Avenue, ensuring that future development would include affordable housing, in addition to mandated onsite stormwater retention to relieve Gowanus’ CSOs.

Gowanus remained largely outside of the wave of “brownstoning” that transformed adjacent neighborhoods. It is home to two public housing campuses–Gowanus Houses and Wyckoff Houses, both the result of brownstone razing to create NYCHA’s signature superblocks (Osman, 2011). But in recent decades, Gowanus has become a focal point for both environmental remediation and residential redevelopment. The area has undergone federal Superfund designation, large-scale rezonings, and public-private partnerships.

The built character of Park Slope, which steeply slopes downhill from Prospect Park to Gowanus, essentially charts the socioeconomic status by grade: the grandest houses are at the top of the hill, with middle-class homes sloping downward, and working-class homes for those working in Gowanus towards the bottom of the hill. (See Figure 5.)

Progressing into the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Park Slope developed into a well-to-do streetcar suburb of Manhattan. By the mid-20th century, parts of the neighborhood had fallen into disrepair, but a wave of middle-class reinvestment in the 1960s and 1970s led to its revival, a process now widely known as "brownstoning." (LPC, 2016).

This was by design. Edwin Clark Litchfield, a prominent railroad magnate, acquired large tracts of land in the mid-19th century, including what is now Prospect Park. His home, Litchfield Villa (1857), remains a historic landmark within Prospect Park, housing the Brooklyn Office of the NYC Department of Parks and Recreation (pictured on the right), and Litchfield developed many of the rowhouse blocks leading up to his mansion for his friends and family (Alexiou, 2015). Litchfield’s vision was to serve multiple housing markets in the then-burgeoning City of Brooklyn: the wealthy next to a hilltop park well above the pollution from Gowanus; the working class next to the industries of Gowanus, with their noise, fumes, and bustle; and the middle class in between.

Public Library Although Park Slope has since absorbed periodic bursts of apartment construction—most visibly along Prospect Park West and upper Eighth Avenue in the 1920s through 1950s—the neighborhood still largely mirrors Edwin Litchfield’s mid-19th century, top-of-the-hill-to-creek vision.

Luxury elevator buildings, such as 9 Prospect Park West (1929), which first introduced high-end flats facing the park, and 90 Eighth Avenue, “The President” (1927), layered density onto the already elite northeast ridge without disturbing the fundamental social gradient sloping down toward Gowanus. Below that ridge, the brownstone mid-blocks, protected by historic district designations and contextual rezonings, have experienced relatively little redevelopment pressure. Constrained capacity on these coveted blocks has instead funneled growth to Fourth Avenue, which was rezoned R8A in 2003. That corridor, in turn, helped justify the 2021 Gowanus rezoning just downhill. Litchfield’s original hierarchy—grand houses atop the park-side bluff, middle-class rows on the slope, and working housing at the industrial waterfront—thus remains legible today, even as property values have risen across every rung of the hill.

These adjoining neighborhoods share similar Italianate and Greek Revival housing stock but have distinct histories. Carroll Gardens features several blocks with deep front gardens. Its small historic district (comprising only 160 buildings over a few blocks) features both the uniquely set-back lots and smaller houses, typically three stories tall, of Italianate and Greek Revival style.

The Carroll Gardens Historic District (1973) makes up only five percent of the neighborhood, but the rest has been contextually rezoned (100 percent of the neighborhood is included in the 2009 rezoning).
By comparison, Cobble Hill’s historic district (established in 1969, with a one-lot extension in 1988) comprises roughly 90 percent of its neighborhood footprint.

Both neighborhoods were heavily shaped by Italian-American communities well into the 20th century. Together with Red Hook and Columbia Street, they were once referred to as “South Brooklyn” (as in south of Brooklyn Heights). Carroll Gardens was a name adopted in the 1970s to differentiate its Cobble Hill-like residential character from that of Gowanus, with which it was previously associated and sought to distinguish itself (Alexiou, 2015). By the start of the 21st century, these neighborhoods were fully gentrified and are now among the most affluent in New York City.
This area is sometimes characterized as Carroll Gardens or Cobble Hill, and sometimes characterized as Red Hook.
Built between 1939 and 1941, the new Brooklyn-Queens Expressway (BQE or I-287)
severed it from Carroll Gardens and Cobble Hill; previously, this neighborhood was indistinguishable both physically and demographically from those two neighborhoods.
Subsequently, while Carroll Gardens and Cobble Hill remained ethnically Italian and gentrified early compared to the rest of Brooklyn, Columbia Street became increasingly Latino.

While Hamilton Avenue and the elevated Gowanus Expressway (a part of the BQE) above it split Red Hook from Carroll Gardens, Red Hook and Columbia Street are seamlessly connected by the Brooklyn Marine Terminal, which runs north to south along the entire Columbia Street waterfront and extends well into Red Hook. (See the next section for more discussion about the Brooklyn Marine Terminal.)

While the area had experienced substantial disinvestment and depopulation, with a notable exodus of Black residents noted in U.S. Census data between 2000 and 2022, it has undergone slow revitalization in the 1990s and 2000s, followed by gentrification in the 2010s and 2020s, driven by small-scale residential and commercial rehabilitation and development. Adjacent to this neighborhood, Brooklyn Bridge Park was developed in the 2010s, converting the piers to the north of the neighborhood into a destination park, thereby enhancing the area's marketability for housing.

In the 19th century, Red Hook became one of the most significant shipping hubs in New York City. With its deep-water docks and waterfront warehouses, the area became a center of maritime commerce. The construction of the Atlantic Basin in the 1840s provided state-of-the-art shipping facilities, solidifying Red Hook’s role in global trade (Spellen, 2015). Red Hook’s industrial landscape supported dense working-class settlement patterns, cementing the neighborhood’s identity as a hub of blue-collar labor and maritime activity into the mid-20th century.

By the mid-20th century, the area faced significant challenges as major industries began to decline. Red Hook, once a thriving shipping hub, saw its docks fall into disuse as containerized shipping emerged, favoring larger, more modern ports with freight access in New Jersey. The closure of the Atlantic Basin’s cargo operations and the decline of nearby shipyards led to thousands of workers becoming unemployed, contributing to economic stagnation in the area. Red Hook had become synonymous with urban decline—economically marginalized, physically isolated, and infrastructurally neglected (Alexiou, 2015). Despite this, it remained home to a resilient community and the Red Hook Houses, the largest NYCHA development in Brooklyn.

Red Hook’s identity has evolved through changes in industrial planning, as well as adaptive reuse and creative-class investment. The 2002 designation of Special Mixed-Use District MX-5 legalized a hybrid of light manufacturing and residential uses along Van Brunt and Beard Streets. With a height cap of 55 feet and limits on hotels and self-storage, MX-5 enabled adaptive reuse conversions such as Fairway Market and Pioneer Works, which now define Red Hook’s industrial-meets-artistic appeal (DCP, n.d.). In 2005, much of the neighborhood was designated part of the Southwest Brooklyn Industrial Business Zone —a Bloomberg-era policy tool aimed at retaining industrial employment. While IBZs don’t impose new zoning, they signal a policy preference for manufacturing and freight uses and provide infrastructure support to industrial tenants. Red Hook remains largely zoned M2-1 and M3-1, for medium to heavy industrial uses. Since the 2010s, however, the industrial mix has shifted. Traditional maritime and construction uses have increasingly given way to “last-mile” logistics: Amazon alone operates two major delivery hubs in the area. Because zoning still classifies these facilities as warehouses, they have proliferated as-of-right, raising environmental justice concerns and prompting CB6 to support the proposed Last-Mile Facility Text Amendment (The City, 2023; CB6, 2024; DCP, 2025).

But Red Hook’s future is increasingly shaped by climate risk. As a low-lying peninsula with a high water table, limited drainage, and porous soils, it faces compounded flood hazards: tidal surges, coastal inundation, and rain-based flooding from extreme precipitation, all of which threaten to be exacerbated by climate change and sea level rise.

During Superstorm Sandy (2012), nearly every block of Red Hook was submerged. Initial flood damage was widespread, but recovery revealed stark contrasts. The Red Hook Houses lost power, heat, and water for weeks. Mold spread, elevators failed, and residents were left in darkness while waiting on emergency generators and temporary boilers (NYCHA, 2022; City Limits, 2024). While also severely flooded, Red Hook’s residential and business hubs outside of NYCHA recovered relatively quickly through private means: insurance payouts, contractor access, and temporary relocation. Within five years, luxury condominiums, cafés, and art galleries had returned or emerged, including $3 million condos at the adaptively reused 160 Imlay Street (The Bridge, 2017), while NYCHA had only just begun recovery construction.

Red Hook’s two-track recovery—one private and rapid, the other public and prolonged—crystallized a key dynamic: climate vulnerability often overlaps with structural inequity. Red Hook Houses received a $560 million FEMA-funded recovery and resiliency project, but bureaucratic delays, construction mismanagement, and pandemic disruptions slowed its progress, with residents coping with intermittent outages and incomplete upgrades for over a decade post-Sandy(City Limits, 2024).

Planning interventions have been piecemeal. The Bloomberg-era SIRR Plan (2013) identified Red Hook as a high-risk zone and proposed an Integrated Flood Protection System (IFPS), but funding never materialized. De Blasio’s Build It Back program excluded NYCHA altogether, focusing on one-to-four family homes. Finally, the Adams administration passed the Red Hook Coastal Resiliency (RHCR) project to construct floodwalls, deployable gates, and raised streets to protect the peninsula. However, RHCR is calibrated only to 2050 sea-level rise scenarios and focuses almost exclusively on coastal surge. It does not account for chronic interior flooding due to Red Hook’s high water table and inadequate drainage—a worsening issue illustrated by rainfall events in 2023 that caused basement flooding across the neighborhood (Brooklyn Eagle, 2023; Politico, 2022).

In 1996, Red Hook: A Plan for Community Regeneration became one of the city’s few officially adopted 197-a plans —a form of neighborhood-driven comprehensive planning allowed under Section 197-a of the New York City Charter. Developed by CB6 in collaboration with DCP, the 197-a plan reflected a community-led vision for equitable growth and public investment in one of Brooklyn’s most under-resourced and environmentally vulnerable neighborhoods.
The plan laid out four long-range goals:
1. Preserve and modernize deep-water maritime and industrial employment
2. Introduce mixed-income housing on suitable inland sites
3. Improve transit access to reduce reliance on trucks and private automobiles
4. Create a continuous, publicly accessible waterfront esplanade (CB6, 1997\)

Announced in 2024 by the New York City Economic Development Corporation (EDC) upon a land swap with the Port Authority of New York-New Jersey, the Brooklyn Marine Terminal (BMT) redevelopment proposes a large-scale redevelopment of Red Hook and Columbia St Waterfront (see Figure 6).

The plan includes approximately 8,000 housing units, a modernized container port, and a new waterfront park and greenway. It is being advanced through a General Project Plan (GPP) by New York State’s Empire State Development Corporation (ESDC)—a state-level mechanism that bypasses ULURP and has drawn criticism for its limited accountability to city agencies or local stakeholders. Furthermore, while new development parcels are slated to receive advanced flood protections, the impacts offsite remain unclear.

Since 2000, rezonings have often served dual purposes: firstly, to protect neighborhood character through contextual controls; secondly, to unlock development opportunities in specific corridors. Prior to the adoption of New York City’s first Zoning Resolution in 1916, CD6 exhibited a strikingly ordered land-use gradient that aligned with both topography and emerging transit infrastructure. High-value single-family row houses and early elevator flats are concentrated along the Prospect Park ridge and Plaza Street. At the same time, progressively narrower brownstones stepped downhill toward the tidal flats of the Gowanus Creek. Heavy industries—coal depots, tanneries, and gasworks—occupied the canal’s edge, taking advantage of waterborne freight and relegating noxious externalities to the district’s lowest elevations. In effect, 19th-century speculative builders and market forces codified a proto-zoning scheme in which elevation, amenity access, and social class were spatially synchronized long before municipal regulation formalized these relationships (Osman, 2011; LPC, 2016). (See Figure 6.)

Despite successive zoning reforms, most of CD6’s 19th-century residential blocks remain virtually unchanged when compared to the 1920 Sanborn fire insurance maps. Notable departures include a concentrated burst of higher-density construction between the 1920s and 1950s in Park Slope in response to subway extensions and heightened demand for elevator living; New Deal and post-war public housing super-blocks—Red Hook Houses (1939), Gowanus Houses (1949), and Wyckoff Gardens (1966)—inserted tower-in-the-park typologies into the row-house grid; and 21st-century upzonings introducing high-rise condos and (largely) mixed-income rentals.

New York City’s 1961 Zoning Resolution—the so-called “second zoning act”—replaced the 1916 height-setback code with the modern floor-area-ratio (FAR) system. For CD6, the rewrite had two lasting consequences: (1) it locked low FAR ceilings (1.6–2.0) onto most brownstone blocks, functionally preserving their scale; and (2) it retained heavy-industrial M-district designations along the Gowanus Canal, Gowanus Bay, and Buttermilk Channel waterfronts, thereby postponing large-scale residential redevelopment there for another six decades. In effect, the 1961 code codified the district’s early 20th-century land-use gradient, reinforcing a built environment that has changed only incrementally since.

Contextual zoning refers to zoning designations that regulate the height, bulk, and street alignment of new buildings to ensure they match the existing built form of a neighborhood. These districts—such as R6A, R6B, or R7A—were introduced in 1987 and widely applied in under Mayor Bloomberg in the 2000s. This is further expounded in the literature review.

Mandatory Inclusionary Housing (MIH) is a city policy adopted in 2016 under Mayor De Blasio that requires permanently affordable housing in new residential developments when a rezoning increases residential floor area. MIH only applies in areas where it has been mapped through a City Council-approved zoning change and affects projects with more than 10 units or 12,500 square feet of residential space.

Universal Affordability Preference (UAP), adopted as part of Mayor Adams’ City of Yes for Housing Opportunity, allows developments to build at least 20% more housing if the additional units are permanently affordable. UAP aims to expand affordable housing opportunities across all medium- to high-desnity neighborhoods by offering targeted density bonuses for projects that include income-restricted units.

CB6 has evolved from protective stances in the early 2000s to a more equity-oriented lens in recent years. CB6 supported downzonings in Park Slope and Carroll Gardens, reflecting resident concerns about bulk, shadows, and out-of-context development. Over time, due largely to turnover of board members and a new District Manager in 2018, the board has increasingly emphasized equity and climate resilience, endorsing the Gowanus Neighborhood Plan in 2021 despite vocal opposition from anti-development factions. Notably, the CB6 passed every action in Figure 7 from 2003 onwards, with the one exception of Atlantic Yards/Pacific Park (2009), where board approval was not a deciding factor in the GPP.

LITERATURE REVIEW New York City's housing crisis sits at the intersection of multiple contested terrains: debates over supply-side versus targeted state interventions, the tension between historic preservation and housing equity, and the spatial distribution of both opportunity and environmental risk. This literature review examines how zoning policies, historic preservation mechanisms, and housing production strategies have shaped and been shaped by competing visions of urban justice and neighborhood change, which can reductively be described “YIMBY” versus “NIMBY” (respectively “yes …” and “not …” in my backyard.

Simultaneously, New York's robust preservation regime, conceived initially as a tool for protecting architectural heritage and neighborhood character, has increasingly been scrutinized for its role in maintaining exclusionary landscapes of privilege. These regulatory frameworks do not operate in isolation but interact to create what scholars term "riskscapes"—geographies where environmental vulnerability, housing access, and regulatory protection are unevenly distributed along lines of race, class, and political power. By synthesizing research on zoning reform, historic preservation, housing adaptability, and environmental justice, this review sheds light on how ostensibly neutral planning tools can perpetuate structural inequities, while also identifying emerging approaches that aim to balance preservation, production, and equity in one of the world's most complex housing markets.

Debates surrounding solutions to housing affordability center on two contrasting ideologies: supply-side advocates (YIMBY, supply-side progressivism) and supply skeptics (NIMBY, tenant advocates, preservationists, critical urban theorists, and social housing proponents).

Supply-side proponents argue that increasing overall housing production, primarily through zoning reform and density allowances, can alleviate affordability pressures across income levels. This perspective relies on basic economic functions, such as meeting demand with supply, as well as mechanisms like filtering, wherein newer, higher-end units indirectly make older units more affordable. It also attributes restrictive zoning to housing supply shortages and adverse impacts on affordability as a result (Been et al., 2018). Ezra Klein’s buzzy book, Abundance (2025), advances this discussion by framing the housing crisis as part of a broader scarcity paradigm—one rooted in institutional inertia and an aversion to growth. Klein argues that constraints on production, ranging from outdated zoning laws to overly procedural governance structures, reflect a deeper political failure to envision and facilitate abundance. His emphasis on "supply-side progressivism" aligns with YIMBY calls for more housing, but also insists that abundance must be equitable, sustainable, and democratically governed. In this framework, housing policy becomes a question not just of supply, but of systems design—how to build institutions that facilitate collective flourishing rather than ossify privilege. His arguments reinforce the need to dismantle regulatory bottlenecks while embedding pro-housing reforms within a justice-oriented political project.

Conversely, “supply skeptics” (Been et al, DATE) contend that merely adding market-rate housing often fails to benefit the most vulnerable populations and may even exacerbate displacement in high-demand areas. They advocate for targeted interventions, such as expanding rental vouchers, preserving existing affordable housing, or investing in public and non-market housing. Critical theorists, such as Marcuse and Madden (2016), challenge the notion that markets alone can resolve structural inequity, arguing instead for decommodified housing models that prioritize equitable access over market-driven production. Fair housing organizations and anti-displacement coalitions argue that without robust tenant protections and proactive equity planning, production-driven strategies can perpetuate and exacerbate racial and class-based disparities (Gurstein & Hertz, 2022; Right to the City Alliance, 2020). Public housing advocates emphasize the inadequacy of market solutions, instead calling for state-built or cooperative housing alternatives. Even among economists, there is skepticism about the filtering model’s adequacy in high-demand cities. Bratt (2006) and others highlight that filtering is often too slow and unreliable to meet the immediate affordability needs of extremely low-income households. Meanwhile, cultural heritage advocates worry that new development may erase valuable social and historic fabric, preferring more nuanced or localized planning responses.

This ideological divide underscores the broader questions about the efficacy and equity of housing policies in addressing affordability and spatial justice, as well as the distinction between real estate markets that are dislocated from housing needs (Madden & Marcuse, 2016). Thus, this study intersects with an already active and hotly contested debate, which will be further explored in the literature review.

secs.t: The Right to the City and The Just City
c: Housing equity in New York City can be viewed through the lens of critical urban theory, notably the "right to the city" framework first articulated by Henri Lefebvre (1968) and popularized by David Harvey. Harvey defines the right to the city as "the right to change ourselves by changing the city," asserting a collective claim to urban space beyond market logics. Susan Fainstein's (2010) "just city" approach similarly argues for planning that prioritizes equity and democracy. These frameworks demand that all urban residents—especially historically marginalized groups—have a voice in land-use decisions and fair access to housing and urban opportunities (Marcuse, 2009; Fainstein, 2010).

Marcuse and Madden further expand this framing in In Defense of Housing (2016), contending that housing must be treated as a social good rather than a commodity and that crisis is not an aberration but a permanent feature of capitalist urbanization. They argue that exclusionary zoning, disinvestment, and redevelopment patterns are not policy failures but deliberate outcomes of a system that prioritizes exchange value over use value. This lens sets up an understanding of housing scarcity as a structural feature, not an accident, underscoring the urgent need to reshape urban planning systems toward redistribution and inclusion.

Zoning has long been a pivotal tool in New York City’s land-use planning, wielding significant influence over housing growth and neighborhood demographics. Research shows that zoning decisions can inadvertently (or deliberately) entrench socioeconomic divides. During the Bloomberg administration (2002–2013), the City rezoned vast swaths of land—over 120 rezonings covering nearly 40 percent of the city—with an eye toward “protecting neighborhood character” in many established areas while encouraging growth in select districts. A Furman analysis found that of approximately 188,000 lots rezoned between 2003 and 2007, only 14 percent were upzoned (allowed for increased housing capacity), whereas 23 percent were downzoned (allowed for reduced density); the remainder were “contextual” rezonings, which limited building form without significant changes in capacity. The net effect of all these changes was a mere 1.7 percent increase in the city’s overall housing capacity, undermining the potential for substantial new housing in a growing city.

Equally important is where these changes happened. The Furman study noted that upzoned areas were disproportionately less white and lower-income, while downzoned or tightly constrained areas were whiter, wealthier, and had higher homeownership rates. In other words, predominantly affluent neighborhoods successfully sought to “reinforce” their existing character (often through height limits and contextual zoning). In contrast, lower-income communities of color were more often asked to absorb growth (and its attendant pressures). Scholars have characterized this pattern as a form of “exclusionary zoning” at the urban scale (Angotti, 2008; Been et al., 2014), as policies purportedly aimed at neighborhood character often align with lines of race and class. Community advocates cite these disparities as evidence that land-use policy has privileged the voices of historically advantaged neighborhoods, enabling them to insulate themselves from change even as other areas face new luxury development and displacement pressures.

The resulting paradox is that zoning aimed at preservation can itself produce inequitable outcomes by limiting new housing in high-demand, high-opportunity districts while deflecting development to fewer, often more vulnerable, neighborhoods. This dynamic is central to understanding New York City’s struggles with housing production and equity.

Contextual rezonings impose height caps, setback requirements, and design rules (without necessarily reducing the allowed Floor Area Ratio (FAR)), aiming to ensure new buildings “fit” their context (DPC, n.d.). While technically race- and class-neutral, these regulations have significant socio-demographic impacts. In a recent difference-in-differences study, Dublin-Boc (2023) examined these rezonings between 1987 and 2019 and found that neighborhoods given contextual zoning protections subsequently grew more affluent and whiter relative to comparable areas without such restrictions. This quantitative evidence suggests that character-focused zoning, defined as the constriction of new construction to maintain the existing street scale, material, and rhythm (Allison and Peters, 2011; Dublin-Boc, 2023), contributes to exclusivity. After implementation, contextually zoned neighborhoods saw rises in income and home values accompanied by an accelerating loss of racial diversity, “entrenching white isolation” and privilege. Dublin-Boc concludes that contextual rezonings, even if classified otherwise and intended to be , are in practice “downzonings.” These findings reinforce earlier observations that downzoning or other anti-growth actions often correlate with the influence of upper-income homeowners, insulating their communities from change.

Importantly, Dublin-Boc’s research ties together the threads of zoning and preservation, noting that both contextual zoning and historic districting are rooted in the notion of protecting neighborhood character, and both can function as exclusionary mechanisms under the banner of NIMBYism. Contextual rezonings during the Bloomberg era often went together with historic district designations. For instance, rowhouse neighborhoods in brownstone Brooklyn and parts of Queens were simultaneously designated as historic districts and rezoned to prevent taller buildings, a double layer of defense against development. This tandem approach appeased local activists concerned about teardowns and out-of-scale apartment buildings. Still, at a citywide scale, it meant fewer new housing units in precisely those neighborhoods most desired for their amenities and transit access.

The debate over the impact of these policies on neighborhood change is lively. Some scholars argue that limiting new development in stable neighborhoods displaces demand to other areas, fueling gentrification there (a form of “shifting burden”). Others counter that contextual rezonings simply protect residents from predatory development and displacement, and that changes in wealth and racial composition are more due to broader market trends. Notably, Wallach’s work on equitable neighborhood change calls for approaches that channel growth in a way that benefits existing communities – for example, community-led planning that pairs contextual controls with affordable housing requirements and anti-displacement measures. Wallach (2020) suggests that neither a laissez-faire upzoning nor a strict preservationist stance alone will produce equitable outcomes; instead, hybrid strategies are needed so that neighborhood improvements (such as new parks and transit) do not automatically translate into the displacement of vulnerable residents. This echoes findings by Furman (2019), which surveyed how cities nationwide responded to gentrification pressures and found that a mix of tools – from tenant protections and affordable housing preservation to inclusionary zoning and targeted upzoning in wealthier areas – is necessary to foster what one might call “equitable development,” the shepherding of neighborhood growth and change without displacing existing residents.

The key is to recognize that land use decisions redistribute who can live where. Contextual zoning and landmarking have tended to favor incumbent, often privileged residents by preserving their neighborhoods' physical integrity and exclusivity. In contrast, the costs of growth (construction, upheaval, rising rents) have fallen on other communities. A more just approach, scholars argue, would spread the responsibility and benefits of change more evenly across the city’s neighborhoods.

Layered on top of zoning controls, New York City’s robust historic preservation regime adds another dimension to the debate over equity. The NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission (LPC) has designated dozens of historic districts – areas deemed architecturally or culturally significant – which impose restrictions on demolition, new construction, and alterations. The tension between preserving neighborhood character and expanding housing access is especially pronounced in these districts. On one hand, preservationists argue that these designations safeguard the city’s heritage and promote a sustainable built form by reusing buildings, per the adage “the greenest building is the one already built.” They highlight the environmental benefits of avoiding demolition waste and the social value of historic continuity and neighborhood pride (Rodriguez, 2019).

However, a growing body of research suggests that historic designation has frequently overlapped with—and perhaps helped maintain—exclusionary landscapes of privilege. A landmark Furman report by Ellen, McCabe, and Stern (2016) provided a comprehensive portrait of New York City’s historic districts over 50 years. It found that historic district neighborhoods are, on average, whiter and higher-income than other areas, even when controlling for location. In Manhattan, census tracts predominantly within historic districts were 73 percent non-Hispanic white (and only seven percent Black) around 2010, compared to 39 percent white in non-landmarked tracts. Similar, though less stark, racial and economic disparities were observed in the outer boroughs. The housing stock in landmarked districts also tends to be older and pricier, with virtually no new construction to offset unit losses. Indeed, development is constrained – new buildings in historic districts are relatively rare and require special approvals, and even as-of-right projects face strict design limits. As a result, some have voiced concern that landmarking can function as “downzoning by another name,” curbing growth in affluent areas and reducing housing opportunity (Navarro, 2018).

Recent empirical work supports this perspective. Brodheim (2023) conducted a longitudinal analysis of “dwelling unit consolidation” across New York City, questioning whether unit consolidation was significantly concentrated within historic districts. He estimated that since 1970, 100,000 housing units have been lost in rowhouses alone, averaging nearly 2,000 units per year. Although he was unable to draw a causal impact from LPC designations, he found that the practice is prevalent in historic districts where little new housing is built to replace the existing structures that have been removed. For example, four historic districts in Manhattan (Central Park West, Greenwich Village, the Upper East Side, and Mount Morris Park) accounted for 40 percent of all residential unit combinations citywide in Brodheim’s sample. Because LPC regulations prevented significant new development, these areas saw a net loss of housing, exacerbating scarcity.

Brodheim notes that while creating a large home out of two or three smaller units may satisfy individual families, it “can have a devastating impact on a historic district’s housing stock” if not counterbalanced by additions elsewhere. The implication is that historic district designations, and their impact on the surrounding environs, have enabled low-rise, wealthy neighborhoods to physically constrain housing supply – a subtle form of exclusion that unfolds behind the façade of preservation. Each high-end brownstone combination displaces the potential for multiple moderate-income households, a pattern that “doesn’t draw public ire like new construction yet removes homes without anyone noticing” (Brodheim, 2023).

Unlike upzonings, which require public engagement, unit loss through consolidation can occur fast, with little oversight (Brodheim, 2023). This piecemeal, silent transformation leaves building facades unchanged while reducing the interior capacity to house multiple households. The amount of time and resources dedicated to removing versus adding housing are on fundamentally different pathways, expediting loss while slowing down gains. Additionally, the high costs associated with new developments, driven by property values, construction materials, labor, and permitting, further constrain affordability. This shrinking supply of housing intensifies competition in the rental market, driving up prices within these neighborhoods.

New York City’s preservation policy is rooted in two traditions: reverence for 19th-century architecture and resistance to postwar urban renewal. The 1965 founding of the LPC signified a pivot toward preserving not only individual buildings, but also neighborhood “character.” Jane Jacobs’ critique of top-down planning in The Death and Life of Great American Cities (1961) profoundly influenced this shift, emphasizing “the sidewalk ballet”—the informal choreography of vibrant public life that can be fostered in specific built environs. Her advocacy for mixed-use neighborhoods and organic urbanism helped make preservation a social, not just aesthetic, cause. However, what began as a check on demolition has evolved into a vehicle for preventing change in increasingly affluent areas. Jacobs’ principles have been both celebrated and co-opted—used to justify forms of protection that inadvertently limit access and diversity, even when her arguments for historic preservation were rooted in assumptions of enhanced affordability and the urban mix (Mallach, 2022).

The role of historic preservation in equity debates is complex and contested. Some planners argue that preservation can serve as a tool for community stabilization in gentrifying areas – a means for longtime residents to assert control over land use and prevent wholesale redevelopment (Dolnick, 2019). There are cases of community-based organizations in New York City’s communities of color pursuing historic district designations to explicitly combat displacement and speculative development (LPC, 2024). However, this strategy may be a double-edged sword: while intended to protect residents, it aligns with homeowner interests and can inadvertently lock in a neighborhood’s existing social profile.

Landmark designation has public benefits – architectural conservation, cultural heritage, and environmental gains – but it also carries distributional consequences. By favoring the status quo of specific high-income neighborhoods, it can constrain the housing choices of those excluded from those neighborhoods. The challenge, then, is balancing preservation with the “right to housing” in the city, ensuring that celebrating the urban past does not impede a more inclusive urban future.

Preservation activists have bristled against a perceived villainization of historic districts as the harbingers of NIMBYism and housing unaffordability, citing their relatively low percentage of New York City’s overall acreage, promoting the value of architectural heritage both for placemaking and as a source of tourist revenue, and arguing that most historic districts are denser or as dense as the community district in which they are located (BFJ, 2021).

The debate also delimits historic districts as a distinct entity outside of contextually rezoned areas. I argue that viewing those regulatory constraints in tandem and within their more local contexts, rather than collapsing all citywide historic districts, provides a much clearer picture of local markets and who can participate in them.

Recent work by Ellen and Kazis (2022) in their report Flexibility and Conversions in New York City’s Housing Stock underscores how New York City’s regulatory environment has restricted the ability to adapt housing forms to changing needs. Their analysis highlights a paradox: while demand for smaller units and multi-household arrangements has increased, the housing stock remains largely inflexible due to building code constraints, zoning barriers, and the complexity of altering existing structures, especially in landmarked and contextually zoned districts.

Ellen and Kazis point to underutilized non-residential space and oversized apartments as missed opportunities for conversion. However, these interventions remain rare—not because the need is lacking, but due to the cumulative burden of permitting, LPC approvals, and non-alignment with zoning incentives. Past efforts at adaptive reuse, such as the Loft Law of the 1980s, were narrowly applied—limited to specific artists and manufacturing districts—and were not expanded into a scalable framework for broader affordability or equitable redevelopment. Without a citywide pathway for retrofitting housing to reflect contemporary living arrangements, a significant share of the city’s built environment remains frozen in time, even as housing pressures intensify.

Brodheim (2023) situates this rigidity within the historical context of housing policy, arguing that many of the City's land-use and building regulations were devised during a time when housing surplus, rather than scarcity, was the perceived problem. These outdated frameworks now hinder the potential for subdivision, retrofitting, and infill that could help address today's housing crisis. Brodheim’s analysis of unit consolidations in historic districts reveals a net loss of housing units as wealthy owners merge formerly multifamily homes into single residences—a trend enabled by a permissive regulatory environment for luxury alterations but prohibitive rules for affordable conversions.

A growing body of literature emphasizes that townhouses and brownstones, especially in the city’s older neighborhoods, are inherently flexible housing types that could be retrofitted to accommodate additional units. Their generous lot sizes, internal staircases, and structural simplicity make them ideal candidates for subdivision, basement apartments, or ADUs (accessory dwelling units) (Ellen & O’Flaherty, 2021; Furman, 2023). However, most historic districts continue to block such changes due to rigid interpretations by the LPC and NYC Department of Buildings of what constitutes appropriateness. Academic literature on ADUs points to their potential as “gentle density”—small-scale additions that preserve neighborhood character while increasing housing supply and diversifying tenure (Chapple et al., 2020). Yet in New York City, ADUs remain largely unpermitted in landmarked neighborhoods, even after the passage of City of Yes.

The city’s history with Single Room Occupancy (SRO) housing further illustrates the consequences of regulatory inflexibility. In the mid-20th century, SROs provided over 200,000 units, offering deeply affordable housing for single adults and very low-income tenants (DCP, 2024). However, from the 1950s through the 1980s, many SROs were systematically eliminated under the banner of slum clearance, at a time when the city faced depopulation, declining rent rolls, and widespread neglect. SRO closures were not simply a function of stigma—they were often a response to real and serious health, safety, and habitability concerns (NYT, 1994). Scholars now widely recognize that the eradication of SRO housing significantly contributed to the rise of homelessness in the city (Sullivan & Burke, 2013; Pinto, 2024), arguing that the eradication of SROs removed an essential rung on the housing ladder—one that had served a vital role in both immigrant communities and neighborhoods facing economic transition. Recent zoning reforms reflect a growing awareness of this history. The City of Yes amendment includes provisions to legalize new rooming-unit housing and micro-units under specific circumstances. Advocacy groups like Open New York and Furman argue that enabling these small-scale formats—ADUs, subdivided brownstones, or SRO-style shared housing—is essential to improving housing equity. However, any revival of SRO models must reckon with the trade-offs: the potential benefits of affordable, flexible housing must be balanced with enforceable safeguards, strong habitability standards, and oversight mechanisms to prevent exploitation.

Davies et al. (2019) define “riskscapes” as political geographies of uneven exposure to harm—landscapes in which environmental risk is distributed along lines of social and spatial inequality, where the distribution of risk is not only a matter of physical vulnerability but is deeply influenced by sociopolitical decision-making and power dynamics.

In New York City, preservation-protected uplands tend to be climate-resilient and amenity-rich, yet highly exclusionary due to landmarking and restrictive zoning. Meanwhile, new housing production has often been concentrated in lower-lying neighborhoods that face increased exposure to flooding and environmental hazards. This sorting of people and risk reflects not only market failure, but also regulatory design. Zoning, preservation, and development incentives jointly shape a city where low-income communities disproportionately bear climate vulnerability.

This spatial mismatch between environmental security and housing opportunity echoes what Madden and Marcuse (2016) describe as the "politics of crisis"—a regime where systemic inequalities are treated as exceptional rather than endemic. By this logic, flood vulnerability and housing precarity are both symptoms of a broader system that prioritizes real estate value over social need. Risk, in this framework, is not randomly distributed but deliberately displaced.

Scholars of environmental justice have similarly noted that land-use and planning decisions, from exclusionary zoning to the siting of resilience infrastructure, reinforce structural inequities by channeling risk away from protected zones and toward marginalized populations. Litwin (2024) observes that even within ostensibly equity-oriented initiatives, such as the City’s Mandatory Inclusionary Housing wherein upzoning is coupled with mandates to provide a modicum or more of affordable housing, most 100 percent affordable projects have been in neighborhoods with existing environmental vulnerabilities. These projects have gravitated to locations where the acquisition of property is less expensive than the norm, there is less competition from developers of market-rate housing, and there is less or no opposition from residents who are empowered by wealth and connections.

Between 2010 and 2024, Brooklyn Community District 6 (CD6) lost over 1,500 units through legal alterations—more than any other community district in Brooklyn and the fourth-highest total citywide, after Manhattan CDs 2, 3, and 8 (DCP, 2025). Nearly all this unit loss occurred within landmarked or contextually downzoned areas, primarily in Park Slope, Carroll Gardens, and Cobble Hill. This data also shows the rapidity of consolidations since the onset of COVID-19 (2020-2024), when CD6 lost 388 units to alteration, more units than any other community district in the city (DCP, 2025).
Entering the 21st century, CD6 experienced slower housing growth than much of the city, but in recent years production has begun to ramp up, largely due to the upzonings of Fourth Avenue and Gowanus.
